Machine learning: Teaching a model to find patterns in historical data so it can make predictions on new data. In this course the model learns to tell fraudulent credit-card transactions apart from legitimate ones.
PDI: Pentaho Data Integration — the ETL platform used throughout the course to orchestrate the machine-learning workflow: preparing data, calling H2O and R, training models, and scoring new transactions.
Spoon: The desktop design tool for building and running PDI transformations and jobs. You use it to run autoML.ktr, train the model, and predict fraud.
Transformation: A PDI data-flow made of steps connected by hops, saved as a .ktr file. The labs use transformations such as autoML.ktr, tr_train_model_fraud.ktr, and tr_predict_fraud.ktr.
Job: A PDI orchestration unit (.kjb) that sequences transformations and other tasks. jb_fraud_main_job.kjb ties the training and prediction transformations together.
Fraud detection: The course's central use case — identifying credit-card transactions that are fraudulent, a problem where losses are high and genuine fraud is rare compared with normal activity.
H2O: An open-source machine-learning platform whose AutoML feature is used to automatically search for well-performing models without extensive manual tuning.
AutoML: Automated machine learning — letting H2O try many algorithms and settings, then rank them, so you can shortlist strong candidate models instead of hand-building each one.
Leaderboard: The ranked table H2O AutoML produces, listing the candidate models it trained ordered by a chosen metric so you can pick the best performer.
Supervised learning: Training a model on labelled historical examples — transactions already marked fraud or legitimate — so it can learn the patterns that distinguish the two and predict the label for new rows.
Unsupervised learning: Finding structure in unlabelled data, used here to surface new, previously unseen kinds of fraud by spotting transactions that do not fit normal patterns.
Imbalanced dataset: A dataset where one class is far rarer than the other, as with fraud being a tiny fraction of all transactions. Handling this imbalance properly is a key focus so the model does not simply ignore the rare cases.
Feature: An individual input column the model learns from, such as transaction amount or billing details. Good features carry the signal the model needs to separate fraud from legitimate activity.
Feature engineering: Creating new, more useful input columns from the raw data so the model has better signal to learn from. The AutoML lab includes a feature-engineering step before model search.
Data wrangling: Cleaning and reshaping the raw data — joining customer, billing, and transaction files into the tidy table the model expects — before any training happens.
Target: The column the model is trying to predict, here whether a transaction is fraudulent. Also called the label.
Label: The known answer attached to each historical example — fraud or legitimate — that supervised learning uses to train and to measure how well the model did.
Training set: The portion of data the model learns from. Its patterns are fitted to these rows.
Test set: Data held back from training and used to check how the model performs on examples it has not seen, giving an honest estimate of real-world accuracy.
Train/test split: Dividing the data into a training portion and a held-back test portion so model quality is measured on unseen rows rather than the data it memorised.
Cross-validation: Repeatedly splitting the data into training and validation folds and averaging the results, giving a more reliable estimate of performance than a single split.
Model training: The process of fitting a model's internal parameters to the training data so it captures the relationship between the features and the target.
Scoring: Applying a trained model to new transactions to produce predictions — here, a fraud probability or label for each incoming order. Also called prediction.
Model artifact: The saved trained model file produced after training, which is loaded later to score new data without retraining. The AutoML lab saves the best model artifact.
Gradient Boosting: The algorithm (GBM) H2O's results point to for this dataset. It builds many small decision trees in sequence, each correcting the errors of the last, to form a strong combined predictor.
GBM: Gradient Boosting Machine — the supervised model trained in R in the credit-card lab using the gbm package to predict fraudulent transactions.
Hyperparameter: A setting that controls how a model learns, fixed before training rather than learned from data. For GBM these include the number of trees, interaction depth, and shrinkage.
Shrinkage: The GBM learning rate that scales each tree's contribution. Smaller values learn more slowly but often generalise better, at the cost of needing more trees.
Overfitting: When a model learns the training data too closely, including its noise, and then performs poorly on new data. Cross-validation and a held-out test set help detect it.
Evaluation metric: A number summarising how good a model's predictions are, used to compare candidates and choose one. Which metric matters depends on the cost of each kind of mistake.
Confusion matrix: A table counting correct and incorrect predictions broken down by class — true and false positives and negatives — from which most fraud metrics are derived.
Accuracy: The fraction of predictions that are correct. On imbalanced fraud data it is a trap, because predicting legitimate for every row can look highly accurate yet catch no fraud.
Precision: Of the transactions the model flags as fraud, the proportion that really are fraud. High precision means fewer false alarms and less customer friction.
Recall: Of all the truly fraudulent transactions, the proportion the model catches. High recall means fewer missed frauds; prioritise it when fraud losses are expensive.
AUC: Area Under the ROC Curve — a single number measuring how well the model ranks fraud above legitimate transactions. Useful as a sanity check, but it can look good even when precision is poor at usable thresholds.
AUCPR: Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve — the best single-number metric for highly imbalanced classification like fraud, used to compare candidate models before tuning thresholds.
Decision threshold: The probability cut-off above which a scored transaction is labelled fraud. Lowering it catches more fraud but raises more false alarms; you tune it to balance precision and recall for the business.
Google Colab: A free service that runs Jupyter notebooks in the browser with preconfigured ML runtimes. You upload the H2O.csv produced by PDI and run the AutoML model search there.
rJava: An R package providing a bridge between R and Java, required so PDI can run R steps. Setup involves configuring R with javareconf and copying libjri into Spoon's native library folder.
R Script Executor: A PDI step that runs R code inside a transformation, used in the prerequisites to validate the R integration and in the credit-card lab to train and apply the GBM model.
